questions.stem: Which term refers to the developmental anomaly that arises when a single tooth germ attempts to divide and results in the incomplete formation of two teeth?
questions.explanation: Gemination is an attempt of ONE tooth germ to divide, giving a bifid crown with a single root and a normal tooth count. Fusion is the joining of TWO germs, so the count is reduced by one.

questions.stem: Which tooth is the most common supernumerary tooth?
questions.explanation: The mesiodens, between the maxillary central incisors, is the most common supernumerary tooth.

questions.stem: Which term refers to a developmental anomaly in which teeth exhibit elongated, large pulp chambers and short roots?
questions.explanation: Taurodontism ('bull teeth') shows an elongated, enlarged pulp chamber with an apically displaced floor and short roots, mainly in molars.

questions.stem: Union of two adjacent teeth by cementum only is known as:
questions.explanation: Concrescence is the union of two adjacent teeth by cementum ONLY, after root formation. Fusion joins dentin and/or enamel.

questions.stem: Ectodermal dysplasia affects all of the following structures except:
questions.explanation: Ectodermal dysplasia affects ectodermal structures: hair, nails, teeth, sweat glands and skin. Bone is mesodermal, so it is not affected.

questions.stem: Pseudo-anodontia is one of the features of:
questions.explanation: In cleidocranial dysplasia permanent and supernumerary teeth form but fail to erupt, so the mouth looks toothless: pseudo-anodontia.

questions.stem: Lack of secondary cementum is one of the dental manifestations of cleidocranial dysplasia.
questions.explanation: True. Teeth in cleidocranial dysplasia lack secondary (cellular) cementum, which is one reason they fail to erupt.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has only the deciduous canines and the first molars. There was neither a history of trauma nor were there missing teeth that were extracted. The child had light fine hair, fair complexion and a facial appearance of an older person. This condition most likely represents:
questions.explanation: Very few teeth (hypodontia), fine light hair, fair skin and an 'aged' face are classic hereditary (hypohidrotic) ectodermal dysplasia.

questions.stem: All the following are clinical features of Streeter's syndrome, except:
questions.explanation: Streeter's syndrome (the course's name for this ectodermal condition) causes xerostomia, dry skin and defective nails with MISSING teeth (hypodontia), not hyperdontia.

questions.stem: A trauma to a tooth may lead to:
questions.explanation: Trauma to a developing tooth can displace the formed part, so the rest of the tooth continues at an angle: dilaceration. Hutchinson's incisors are from congenital syphilis.

questions.stem: Talon cusp is most commonly seen:

options.text: On the lingual surface of the lower permanent incisors
On the occlusal surface of upper permanent molars
On the lingual surface of upper permanent incisors
On the occlusal surface of lower permanent molars

questions.explanation: A talon cusp is an extra cusp on the lingual (cingulum) area of the upper permanent incisors, often shaped like an eagle's talon.

questions.stem: Delayed shedding of deciduous teeth and delayed eruption of permanent teeth are seen in:
questions.explanation: Cleidocranial dysplasia causes prolonged retention of deciduous teeth and delayed or failed eruption of the permanent and supernumerary teeth.

questions.stem: Hutchinson's incisors are:

options.text: An acquired condition affecting permanent teeth
A hereditary condition affecting permanent teeth
A hereditary condition affecting both dentitions
An acquired condition affecting only deciduous teeth

questions.explanation: Hutchinson's incisors (screwdriver-shaped, notched incisal edge) are caused by congenital syphilis, an ACQUIRED (infectious) condition, and affect the permanent incisors.

questions.stem: Among the clinical features of Streeter's syndrome:
questions.explanation: Streeter's syndrome in this course includes dry skin, defective nails and xerostomia, so all of the above.

questions.stem: Which location is the most likely for an enamel pearl?
questions.explanation: Enamel pearls are most common on the maxillary molars, usually at the furcation or near the CEJ.

questions.stem: Developmental defects in the shape of teeth are due to disturbances in the:
questions.explanation: Abnormalities of tooth SHAPE arise during morpho-differentiation (bell stage), when the crown pattern is laid down. Initiation affects tooth number; apposition affects structure.

questions.stem: Teeth which exhibit a yellow or brown-gray discoloration and fluoresce bright yellow under ultraviolet light have most probably been affected by:
questions.explanation: Tetracycline binds calcium in the developing teeth, giving yellow to brown-grey discoloration that fluoresces bright yellow under ultraviolet light.

questions.stem: Dentinogenesis imperfecta type III is associated with osteogenesis imperfecta.
questions.explanation: False. Osteogenesis imperfecta is associated with dentinogenesis imperfecta TYPE I. Type II occurs alone, and type III is the Brandywine isolate (shell teeth).

questions.stem: Tetracycline ingestion during tooth development causes:
questions.explanation: Tetracycline taken while teeth are forming causes intrinsic tooth discoloration (yellow-brown, grey).

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions affects both deciduous and permanent teeth?
questions.explanation: Dentinogenesis imperfecta is hereditary, so it affects BOTH dentitions. Turner's tooth, Hutchinson's incisors (congenital syphilis) and talon cusp affect individual permanent teeth.

questions.stem: Turner's tooth is a condition caused by enamel hypoplasia due to:
questions.explanation: Turner's tooth is a localized enamel hypoplasia of a permanent tooth caused by periapical infection or trauma of the overlying deciduous tooth.

questions.stem: Hereditary teeth defects affect all teeth while acquired defects affect a single tooth or a group of teeth.

options.text: The 1st statement is false while the 2nd one is correct
The 1st statement is correct while the second one is false

questions.explanation: Both are correct: hereditary defects (e.g. amelogenesis imperfecta) affect all teeth, while acquired defects (e.g. Turner's tooth, local trauma) affect one tooth or a group formed at the same time.

questions.stem: The microorganism primarily responsible for the initiation of dental caries is:
questions.explanation: Streptococcus mutans initiates caries: it is acidogenic, aciduric and makes sticky extracellular glucans (dextran) from sucrose. Lactobacilli are mainly involved in the progression of established lesions.

questions.stem: Contributing factors in dental caries are:

options.text: Susceptible tooth, fermentable carbohydrates, dental plaque and age
Susceptible tooth, saliva, fermentable carbohydrates, micro-organisms and time
Susceptible tooth, saliva, dental plaque, micro-organisms and age
Susceptible tooth, non-fermentable carbohydrates, micro-organisms and time

questions.explanation: Caries needs a susceptible tooth (host), saliva, fermentable carbohydrates, micro-organisms and time. The other options each miss an essential factor or include non-fermentable carbohydrates.

questions.stem: The teeth that are most resistant to caries are:
questions.explanation: Mild fluorosis means the enamel contains more fluorapatite, which is less soluble in acid, so these teeth are the most caries resistant. Hypoplasia, hypocalcification and malposition all increase risk.

questions.stem: The process of dental caries comprises:

options.text: Demineralization of the tooth substance and proteolysis of the softened matrix by microorganisms
Destruction of tooth substance by anaerobic bacteria
Demineralization of enamel and dentin exclusively by acids
Lysis of organic tooth substances by proteolytic bacteria and liquefaction of dentin

questions.explanation: Caries is a two-stage process: acids from bacterial fermentation demineralize the inorganic part of the tooth, then proteolytic bacteria break down the softened organic matrix.

questions.stem: The carbohydrate having the most cariogenic potential is:

options.text: Fructose, because it is a major component in fruits
Sucrose, because of its low molecular weight and easy diffusibility into the plaque
Starch, because of its long monosaccharide chain whose breakdown supplies energy to the cariogenic bacteria
Sucrose, because it acts as a store for carbohydrates
Fructose, because it is sticky and found in honey

questions.explanation: Sucrose is the most cariogenic sugar: its small molecule diffuses easily into plaque, and S. mutans uses it to make sticky extracellular glucans (dextran) that help bacteria adhere.

questions.stem: Regarding dental caries, which of the following is true?

options.text: Lactobacilli are the bacteria that are the main cause of dental caries
Lactobacilli can produce pit and fissure caries

questions.explanation: Lactobacilli can produce pit and fissure caries (in gnotobiotic animal studies) but not smooth surface caries; they are not the main initiators of caries (that is S. mutans), and xylitol is non-cariogenic. Note: 'cariogenic bacteria produce organic acids' is also a true fact, so read this question carefully.

questions.stem: Dextran:

options.text: Is an adhesive water soluble fructose polymer
Is an adhesive water insoluble glucose polymer
Is a non-adhesive water soluble fructose polymer
Is an adhesive water soluble galactose polymer

questions.explanation: Dextran is a glucose polymer that S. mutans makes from sucrose. It is sticky (adhesive) and water-insoluble, so it builds the plaque matrix. Levan is the fructose polymer.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are correct?

options.text: S. mutans are acidogenic and aciduric
S. mutans can produce pit and fissure caries only
S. mutans are transmissible and can produce amylopectin

questions.explanation: S. mutans is acidogenic and aciduric, is transmissible (often from mother to child) and can store intracellular polysaccharide (amylopectin-like). It causes smooth surface caries too, so 'pit and fissure only' is wrong.

questions.stem: The clinical significance of sclerotic dentin is that it is:
questions.explanation: Sclerotic (transparent) dentin forms when tubules are blocked with mineral. It is harder and less permeable, so it is more resistant to caries and acts as a defensive barrier.

questions.stem: Rats raised in a germ-free environment will develop dental caries if:

options.text: Specific strains of cariogenic microorganisms are introduced into their oral cavity associated with feeding with a non-fermentable carbohydrate diet
They are fed a high protein diet
Specific strains of cariogenic microorganisms are introduced into their oral cavity associated with feeding with a high fermentable carbohydrate diet
They are fed a high sugar diet

questions.explanation: Germ-free animals do not get caries. They develop it only when specific cariogenic bacteria are introduced AND they are fed fermentable carbohydrate: both factors are needed.

questions.stem: Gnotobiotic animals are:

options.text: Animals with a known strain of microorganisms
Animals fed with a high CHO diet

questions.explanation: Gnotobiotic animals are animals whose microbial flora is fully known (e.g. germ-free animals inoculated with a known strain). This is how specific bacteria were proven cariogenic.

questions.stem: Gustafson, with the Vipeholm experiment, demonstrated the role of:
questions.explanation: Gustafson's Vipeholm study showed the role of CARBOHYDRATES: sugar eaten between meals and in sticky forms caused far more caries than the same sugar taken with meals.

questions.stem: Contributing factors of dental caries include all of the following, except:
questions.explanation: Caries depends on the host (tooth), saliva, carbohydrate substrate, bacteria and time. Viruses play no role.

questions.stem: The main factor influencing the cariogenicity of carbohydrates is:
questions.explanation: The FREQUENCY of carbohydrate intake matters most: every exposure drops plaque pH below the critical level, so frequent snacking is worse than the same amount eaten at once (Vipeholm).

questions.stem: The pioneer micro-organisms invading dentine are the same pioneer organisms noted in initial dental plaque formation.
questions.explanation: The pioneer bacteria in dentin caries are mainly lactobacilli (and other acidogenic and proteolytic organisms), not the streptococci and actinomyces that first colonize a clean tooth surface.

questions.stem: The cariostatic effect of fluoride is mainly due to all of the following, except:

options.text: Its ability to change the fluoroapatite crystal lattice into the stronger more resistant hydroxyapatite crystal lattice
It facilitates re-mineralization of the tooth structure

questions.explanation: Fluoride converts HYDROXYAPATITE into the more acid-resistant FLUORAPATITE (the option reverses this), promotes remineralization and is bacteriostatic.

questions.stem: Acute (rampant) caries is characteristically seen in:
questions.explanation: Acute (rampant) caries progresses rapidly and is typical of children and young patients; chronic caries progresses slowly and is seen in older adults.

questions.stem: Streptococcus mutans is considered to be the pioneer micro-organism in the initial community of plaque.
questions.explanation: S. mutans is not the pioneer. The first colonizers of a clean pellicle are Streptococcus sanguis and Actinomyces viscosus; S. mutans joins later.

questions.stem: Enamel hypoplasia and enamel hypocalcification:

options.text: Do not have an effect on either the initiation or the progression of dental caries
Affect the rate of initiation, and not the rate of progression of dental caries
Affect the rate of progression, and not the initiation of dental caries

questions.explanation: Enamel hypoplasia and hypocalcification do not start caries by themselves, but once a lesion begins they make it progress faster. They affect the rate of progression, not initiation.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Streptococcus mutans can produce pit and fissure caries only
Streptococcus mutans are acidogenic and aciduric

questions.explanation: S. mutans can produce amylopectin (intracellular storage polysaccharide) AND it is acidogenic and aciduric, so both a and d are correct. It does not cause pit and fissure caries only.

questions.stem: Miller's experiment proved the role of carbohydrates in dental caries.
questions.explanation: False. Miller's chemo-parasitic theory showed that bacteria produce acid that dissolves enamel; the role of dietary carbohydrates was demonstrated by Gustafson's Vipeholm study.

questions.stem: Caries is best defined as progressive, reversible bacterial damage to the hard dental structures present in the oral cavity.
questions.explanation: False. Caries is progressive and IRREVERSIBLE bacterial destruction of the hard dental tissues (only the very early white spot lesion can remineralize).

questions.stem: The arch criminal of dental caries is considered to be:
questions.explanation: Sucrose is the 'arch criminal' of dental caries: it is the substrate S. mutans uses to make acid and sticky dextran.

questions.stem: The critical pH is the pH at which:
questions.explanation: The critical pH (about 5.5) is the pH at which plaque fluid becomes unsaturated with calcium and phosphate, so enamel demineralization starts.

questions.stem: The acquired enamel pellicle is formed of:
questions.explanation: The acquired pellicle is a thin, cell-free film of salivary glycoproteins that forms on a clean tooth within minutes. Bacteria attach to it afterwards to form plaque.

questions.stem: Newly erupted teeth are considered to be more caries susceptible than older ones.
questions.explanation: True. Newly erupted teeth have not completed post-eruptive maturation (enamel is less mineralized and has less fluoride), so they are more susceptible to caries.

questions.stem: Dental caries is defined as

options.text: Progressive, irreversible bacterial destruction of tooth structure

questions.explanation: Caries is progressive, irreversible destruction of tooth structure by bacterial acids. Mechanical wear is attrition/abrasion.

questions.stem: The most common type of dental caries is
questions.explanation: Pit and fissure caries is most common because the fissures trap food and plaque and are hard to clean.

questions.stem: Cemental (root) caries is commonly associated with
questions.explanation: Gingival recession exposes cementum, so root caries is typical of older adults with recession.

questions.stem: Recurrent caries occurs
questions.explanation: Recurrent (secondary) caries starts at the margins of existing restorations.

questions.stem: Acute caries is more common in
questions.explanation: Acute (rampant) caries progresses quickly and is more common in children and young people.

questions.stem: Chronic caries affects mostly
questions.explanation: Chronic caries progresses slowly and is mostly seen in older adults.

questions.stem: Posterior teeth are more susceptible to caries because
questions.explanation: Pits and fissures on posterior teeth retain plaque and food, making them more susceptible.

questions.stem: Enamel hypoplasia affects
questions.explanation: Enamel hypoplasia does not start caries but speeds up its progression once it begins.

questions.stem: Newly erupted teeth are more caries susceptible because
questions.explanation: Newly erupted teeth have not completed post-eruptive maturation, so the enamel is less resistant.

questions.stem: The cariostatic effect of fluoride includes
questions.explanation: Fluoride converts hydroxyapatite into more acid-resistant fluorapatite, promotes remineralization and is bacteriostatic.

questions.stem: Saliva protects against caries mainly by
questions.explanation: Saliva protects mainly by washing (clearance) and buffering acids, besides antibacterial and remineralizing actions.

questions.stem: The antibacterial components of saliva include
questions.explanation: Lysozyme, lactoferrin and the peroxidase system are the antibacterial components of saliva.

questions.stem: Sucrose is considered the ‘arch criminal’ because

options.text: It diffuses rapidly and supports bacterial adhesion

questions.explanation: Sucrose diffuses rapidly into plaque and is used to make sticky extracellular glucans that help bacteria adhere.

questions.stem: Sticky carbohydrates are more cariogenic because

options.text: They remain longer for acid production

questions.explanation: Sticky carbohydrates stay on the teeth longer, so bacteria have more time to make acid.

questions.stem: Refinement of carbohydrates increases caries risk because
questions.explanation: Refining removes fibre, leaving soft, sticky carbohydrate that clings to teeth.

questions.stem: The Vipeholm study concluded that

options.text: Frequency of sugar intake increases caries
Total sugar amount is the main factor

questions.explanation: Vipeholm showed that the FREQUENCY of sugar intake (especially between meals) matters more than the total amount.

questions.stem: Orland’s experiment demonstrated

options.text: Germ-free rats do not develop caries

questions.explanation: Orland showed that germ-free rats do not develop caries even on a high-sugar diet: bacteria are essential.

questions.stem: The main acidogenic bacteria in caries are
questions.explanation: S. mutans and lactobacilli are the main acidogenic (acid-producing) caries bacteria.

questions.stem: Proteolytic bacteria include
questions.explanation: Actinomyces are proteolytic and help break down the organic matrix, especially in root and dentin caries.

questions.stem: Dental plaque is defined as

options.text: A bacterial biofilm adherent to tooth surface

questions.explanation: Dental plaque is a bacterial biofilm firmly adherent to the tooth surface, not just food debris.

questions.stem: The supragingival plaque is located
questions.explanation: Supragingival plaque lies above the gingival margin; subgingival plaque lies below it.

questions.stem: The main inorganic component of plaque is
questions.explanation: Calcium and phosphate are the main inorganic components of plaque.

questions.stem: Plaque matrix retains acids by
questions.explanation: The plaque matrix acts as a diffusion barrier, holding acids against the enamel and keeping saliva's buffers out.

questions.stem: The first bacteria to colonize clean tooth surfaces are
questions.explanation: Streptococcus sanguis and Actinomyces viscosus are the first colonizers of a clean pellicle.

questions.stem: Streptococcus mutans produces
questions.explanation: S. mutans makes extracellular dextran (glucan) and levan (fructan) from sucrose.

questions.stem: Mature plaque shows ‘corn cob’ arrangement formed by
questions.explanation: 'Corn cob' formations in mature plaque are filamentous bacteria (actinomyces) coated by cocci.

questions.stem: Stephan’s curve shows

options.text: Rapid drop in plaque pH after sugar intake

questions.explanation: Stephan's curve shows the rapid drop in plaque pH after a sugar rinse and its slow recovery.

questions.stem: The critical pH for enamel demineralization is approximately
questions.explanation: The critical pH for enamel demineralization is about 5.5.

questions.stem: Early smooth surface caries appears clinically as
questions.explanation: Early smooth surface caries appears as a white, chalky spot (subsurface demineralization).

questions.stem: Arrested enamel caries appears as
questions.explanation: Arrested enamel caries becomes a brown, hard spot as it picks up stain and remineralizes.

questions.stem: The cone of enamel caries has its base toward
questions.explanation: Smooth surface enamel caries forms a cone with its base at the enamel surface and its apex towards the DEJ.

questions.stem: In dentin caries, the cone base is toward
questions.explanation: In dentin, the caries cone has its base at the DEJ and its apex towards the pulp.

questions.stem: The first histological zone of enamel caries is
questions.explanation: The translucent zone is the first, deepest zone of enamel caries (the advancing front).

questions.stem: The surface zone of enamel remains intact because
questions.explanation: The surface zone stays relatively intact because minerals reprecipitate there from saliva and plaque.

questions.stem: Dead tracts in dentin indicate
questions.explanation: Dead tracts are dentinal tubules left empty after the odontoblast processes die.

questions.stem: Liquefaction foci are
questions.explanation: Liquefaction foci are areas where distended dentinal tubules coalesce as the matrix is destroyed.

questions.stem: Transverse clefts form
questions.explanation: Transverse clefts form at right angles to the dentinal tubules in advanced dentin caries.

questions.stem: Sclerotic dentin acts as
questions.explanation: Sclerotic dentin is a defensive barrier: blocked tubules slow down the spread of caries.

questions.stem: The zone of reactionary dentin indicates
questions.explanation: Reactionary (tertiary) dentin is a pulpal defense response laid down beneath the lesion.

questions.stem: If a chronic path of drainage (sinus tract) is established, a periapical abscess becomes asymptomatic.
questions.explanation: Once a sinus tract drains the pus, pressure on the periapical tissues drops, so the abscess becomes asymptomatic (a chronic, draining abscess).

questions.stem: Galvanic shock occurs when two different metallic fillings with different electromotive potential (e.g. gold versus amalgam) placed in opposing arches come in contact, with the saliva acting as a fluid conductor.
questions.explanation: Galvanic shock: two dissimilar metal restorations (e.g. gold and amalgam) in opposing teeth form a battery when they touch, with saliva as the electrolyte, giving a sharp electrical pain.

questions.stem: Histologically, the inflammatory infiltrate seen in periapical granulomas is made up of plasma cells, lymphocytes, neutrophils and rare eosinophils. Foam cells are never seen histologically within periapical granulomas.

options.text: The first statement is correct while the second is incorrect
The first statement is incorrect while the second is correct

questions.explanation: The first statement is right: the infiltrate is plasma cells, lymphocytes, neutrophils and occasional eosinophils. The second is wrong: foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) ARE seen in periapical granulomas, along with cholesterol clefts and giant cells.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female complains of pain in her lower first molar, recently restored with amalgam. The pain is precipitated by heat or cold stimuli and disappears immediately after removal of the stimulus. Clinically there is a large occluso-mesial amalgam filling; radiographically it is deep and close to the pulp, and the periapical area is free of pathosis. Based on these findings, the condition most likely represents:
questions.explanation: Pain triggered by hot or cold that stops as soon as the stimulus is removed, in a tooth with a deep restoration and a healthy periapex, is pulp hyperemia (focal reversible pulpitis). Pain that lingers would be acute pulpitis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female complains of pain in her lower first molar, recently restored with amalgam. The pain is precipitated by heat or cold stimuli and disappears immediately after removal of the stimulus. Clinically there is a large occluso-mesial amalgam filling; radiographically it is deep and close to the pulp, and the periapical area is free of pathosis. To confirm the diagnosis, electrical pulp testing should reveal:

options.text: A higher level of response than the adjacent teeth
A lower level of response than the adjacent teeth
A similar level of response compared to the adjacent teeth

questions.explanation: A hyperemic (inflamed but vital) pulp is hypersensitive, so it responds to electric pulp testing at a LOWER current than the adjacent normal teeth.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female complains of pain in her lower first molar, recently restored with amalgam. The pain is precipitated by heat or cold stimuli and disappears immediately after removal of the stimulus. Clinically there is a large occluso-mesial amalgam filling; radiographically it is deep and close to the pulp, and the periapical area is free of pathosis. If histopathologic examination of the pulpal tissue is conducted, it should reveal:

options.text: Dilated blood vessels with increased blood supply within the involved pulpal tissue
Dilated blood vessels with increased blood supply and an inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of plasma cells and lymphocytes
Dilated blood vessels with increased blood supply and an inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of neutrophils

questions.explanation: Pulp hyperemia histologically shows only dilated, engorged blood vessels (with edema). There is no significant inflammatory cell infiltrate yet; plasma cells and lymphocytes mean chronic pulpitis, neutrophils mean acute pulpitis.

questions.stem: Electric pulp testing of a tooth involved with chronic pulpitis reveals:

options.text: The involved tooth will respond to a higher level than a normal tooth
The involved tooth will respond to a lower level than a normal tooth
The involved tooth fails to respond to pulp testing

questions.explanation: In chronic pulpitis the nerve fibres degenerate, so the tooth needs a HIGHER current than a normal tooth to respond. Acute pulpitis responds at a lower level.

questions.stem: Periapical granuloma can be located:
questions.explanation: A periapical granuloma forms wherever the infected root canal opens: at the apex, laterally along the root (lateral canal) or between the roots (furcation canals).

questions.stem: The prerequisites for chronic hyperplastic pulpitis to occur are:

options.text: A non-vital tooth with a large carious exposure, in an old patient with a well formed root and narrow apical foramen
A vital tooth with a large carious exposure, in a young patient with incomplete root formation and a wide apical foramen

questions.explanation: Chronic hyperplastic pulpitis (pulp polyp) needs a VITAL pulp with a good blood supply: a young patient, an open (wide) apex and a large carious exposure that lets the granulation tissue grow out.

questions.stem: In chronic pulpitis:

options.text: The involved pulpal tissue shows an inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of plasma cells and lymphocytes
The involved pulpal tissue shows an inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of neutrophils
The involved pulpal tissue only shows dilated blood vessels

questions.explanation: Chronic pulpitis shows granulation tissue with a chronic infiltrate of plasma cells and lymphocytes. Neutrophils are typical of acute pulpitis; dilated vessels alone are hyperemia.

questions.stem: Maxillary sinusitis can present clinically as upper posterior teeth pain.
questions.explanation: The roots of the upper posterior teeth lie close to the floor of the maxillary sinus, so sinusitis can refer pain to them (several teeth tender to percussion). Always consider it before treating the teeth.

questions.stem: The process of diapedesis which is seen in acute pulpitis allows for the migration of neutrophils through the blood vessel walls.
questions.explanation: Diapedesis is the passage of white cells (neutrophils in acute inflammation) through intact blood vessel walls into the tissue. It is a key event in acute pulpitis.

questions.stem: Bacteria can reach the pulp through:
questions.explanation: Bacteria reach the pulp through caries (most common), through a fracture or crack in the crown, and via the blood stream to an already inflamed pulp (anachoresis). All three are correct.

questions.stem: All of the following clinical signs and symptoms are seen in cavernous sinus thrombosis except:
questions.explanation: Cavernous sinus thrombosis causes exophthalmos, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, loss of corneal reflexes, fever and DILATED pupils (cranial nerve III involvement). Pin-point (constricted) pupils are not a feature.

questions.stem: Aerodontalgia is the tooth pain caused by a drop in atmospheric pressure as a result of flying at high altitudes. A prerequisite for aerodontalgia is that the tooth or teeth involved most probably has recently received a deep permanent restoration, e.g. a deep amalgam filling.

options.text: The first statement is correct while the second statement is incorrect
The second statement is correct while the first statement is incorrect

questions.explanation: Both statements are correct: aerodontalgia is tooth pain from a drop in atmospheric pressure at altitude, and it usually affects a tooth with a recent deep restoration (an already irritated pulp).

questions.stem: Infection from the dangerous area of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus via:

options.text: Emissary veins in a retrograde fashion

questions.explanation: The facial veins of the 'dangerous area' (upper lip, nose) have no valves, so infection can travel backwards (retrograde) through the emissary/ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus.

questions.stem: The intraoral opening of a draining sinus tract is termed:
questions.explanation: The parulis (gum boil) is the mass of inflamed granulation tissue at the intraoral opening of a sinus tract. A Phoenix abscess is an acute flare-up of a chronic periapical lesion.

questions.stem: Radiographically, a periapical abscess presents as:
questions.explanation: An acute periapical abscess spreads through bone quickly with no time for a sclerotic border, so it appears as an ILL-defined radiolucency (often only a widened PDL early on). A granuloma or cyst is well defined.

questions.stem: A patient presents with severe lancinating pain involving his upper second premolar. The pain increases while lying down and keeps him awake. Hot and cold drinks precipitate the pain, and the tooth remains painful after removal of the stimulus. This patient is most likely suffering from:
questions.explanation: Severe, lancinating pain that wakes the patient, worsens on lying down and LINGERS after the hot/cold stimulus is removed is acute pulpitis (irreversible).

questions.stem: Histopathologically, focal reversible pulpitis exhibits an intact odontoblastic layer, dilated blood vessels and neutrophils.
questions.explanation: Focal reversible pulpitis shows dilated vessels, edema and an intact odontoblastic layer but NO neutrophil infiltrate. Neutrophils mean acute pulpitis, so the statement is false.

questions.stem: Chronic ulcerative pulpitis is a misnomer, owing to the fact that:

options.text: An ulcer is covered by epithelium
An ulcer is defined as a discontinuity of the connective tissue
An ulcer is defined as a discontinuity of the epithelium

questions.explanation: An ulcer is a break in the EPITHELIUM. The pulp is connective tissue with no epithelial covering, so 'ulcerative' pulpitis is a misnomer.

questions.stem: Pulpitis induced by the dentist is termed:
questions.explanation: Pulpitis caused by the dentist (overheating, deep cavity preparation, chemicals) is iatrogenic, or odontoiatrogenic, pulpitis.

questions.stem: The vast majority of dental abscesses perforate the:
questions.explanation: The buccal cortical plate over most teeth is thinner than the lingual, so most dental abscesses perforate buccally. The lower molars are the main exception (thin lingual plate).

questions.stem: The majority of cases of Ludwig's angina develop from the spread of an acute infection from the lower molar teeth as a direct result of:

options.text: The fact that the lingual cortex in this area is thinner than the buccal cortex
The fact that the lingual cortex in this area is thicker than the buccal cortex
The fact that the root apices of these teeth are located below the attachment of the mylohyoid muscle
The fact that the root apices of these teeth are located above the attachment of the mylohyoid muscle

questions.explanation: Ludwig's angina mostly starts from lower molars because (A) the lingual cortex there is thinner than the buccal, and (C) the root apices lie BELOW the mylohyoid attachment, so pus enters the submandibular space.

questions.stem: In acute pulpitis, the tooth responds to electric pulp testing at lower levels of current.
questions.explanation: An acutely inflamed pulp is hyper-reactive, so it responds to electric pulp testing at LOWER current levels than a normal tooth.

questions.stem: When the tooth feels slightly elevated in its socket, this feature is attributed to:
questions.explanation: In a periapical granuloma the inflamed tissue at the apex pushes the tooth slightly out of the socket, so the patient feels it is 'high' and tender on biting.

questions.stem: Bacteria can reach the pulp via all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Bacteria reach the pulp through caries, fractures, the periapical tissues (retrograde via the apex or lateral canals) and the blood (anachoresis). They do NOT travel along nerve fibres.

questions.stem: The pulp polyp is made up of a granulation tissue which is covered by epithelium. The epithelium is derived from the rests of Malassez.

options.text: The first statement is incorrect while the second is correct
The first statement is correct while the second is incorrect

questions.explanation: The first statement is correct: a pulp polyp is granulation tissue that may be covered by stratified squamous epithelium. The second is wrong: the epithelium comes from grafted oral epithelium (desquamated cells from the buccal mucosa/gingiva), not the rests of Malassez.

questions.stem: Severe, lancinating pain that does not disappear after removal of the stimulus is one of the features of:
questions.explanation: Severe, lancinating pain that persists after the stimulus is removed is the hallmark of acute (irreversible) pulpitis.

questions.stem: The tooth responds to electric pulp testing at a higher level than normal in:
questions.explanation: The degenerated nerve fibres in chronic pulpitis need a HIGHER current to respond during electric pulp testing.

questions.stem: In pulp hyperemia, the tooth involved shows:

options.text: Histologically, dilated blood vessels which are engorged with plasma cells and lymphocytes within the involved pulpal tissue
Clinically, pain with hot and cold stimuli which remains after the stimulus is removed
Histologically, dilated blood vessels which are engorged with blood within the involved pulpal tissue

questions.explanation: Pulp hyperemia histologically shows dilated blood vessels engorged with BLOOD. Pain that lingers after the stimulus is acute pulpitis, and a periapical swelling is a periapical lesion.

questions.stem: The treatment of a tooth with acute pulpitis is:

options.text: Filling without a root canal treatment
Performing a root canal treatment or extraction

questions.explanation: Acute pulpitis is irreversible, so the inflamed pulp must be removed: root canal treatment, or extraction if the tooth cannot be restored. A simple filling is not enough.

questions.stem: Chronic hyperplastic pulpitis is commonly referred to as a 'pulp polyp'. The use of this term should be discontinued as it is considered to be a misnomer, owing to the fact that:

options.text: A polyp is a swelling of epithelial origin
A polyp is a swelling of connective tissue origin
A polyp is an acute condition

questions.explanation: A true polyp is a swelling of EPITHELIAL origin, while the pulp polyp is a mass of connective (granulation) tissue, so the term is a misnomer.

questions.stem: Ludwig's angina commonly results from spread of infection from:
questions.explanation: Ludwig's angina usually follows infection of the LOWER POSTERIOR (molar) teeth: their apices lie below the mylohyoid and the lingual plate is thin, so pus spreads into the submandibular space.

questions.stem: An eight-year-old boy presented to your dental office for treatment of a broken down lower right molar. Clinical examination revealed a badly broken down molar with a pink mass protruding from its occlusal surface. The diagnosis of this lesion is:
questions.explanation: A young patient, a badly broken-down molar and a pink mass growing out of the cavity is chronic hyperplastic pulpitis (pulp polyp).

questions.stem: An eight-year-old boy presented to your dental office for treatment of a broken down lower right molar. Clinical examination revealed a badly broken down molar with a pink mass protruding from its occlusal surface. Based on your diagnosis, histopathologically this lesion is composed of:

options.text: Granulation tissue exhibiting an inflammatory infiltrate composed of plasma cells and lymphocytes
Granulation tissue exhibiting an inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils
Granulation tissue covered by stratified squamous epithelium

questions.explanation: A pulp polyp is granulation tissue with plasma cells and lymphocytes (chronic inflammation) and it may be covered by stratified squamous epithelium, so 'a and c' is the answer.

questions.stem: An eight-year-old boy presented to your dental office for treatment of a broken down lower right molar. Clinical examination revealed a badly broken down molar with a pink mass protruding from its occlusal surface. A periapical radiograph reveals the badly decayed molar with a wide carious exposure. The diagnosis of this lesion is:
questions.explanation: A young patient, a pink mass protruding from a wide carious exposure in a molar is chronic hyperplastic pulpitis (pulp polyp). The ulcerative type has no protruding mass.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most definitive in distinguishing a periapical granuloma from a periapical cyst?
questions.explanation: A granuloma and a cyst look similar radiographically and clinically (both on non-vital teeth). Only histopathology can tell them apart: an epithelium-lined cavity means a cyst.

questions.stem: The phenomenon in which bacteria circulating in the blood tend to localize in an inflamed area is known as:
questions.explanation: Anachoresis is the localization of blood-borne bacteria in an inflamed area (such as an inflamed pulp). Diapedesis is the movement of white cells through vessel walls.

questions.stem: Toothache occurring in personnel of air crews when flying at high altitudes or entering a low pressure chamber is termed:
questions.explanation: Aerodontalgia is toothache caused by reduced atmospheric pressure (flying, pressure chambers), usually in teeth with an already inflamed pulp or recent deep restorations.

questions.stem: Infection from the dangerous area of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus via:

options.text: Emissary veins in a retrograde fashion

questions.explanation: The valveless veins of the dangerous area of the face allow retrograde spread of infection through the emissary veins into the cavernous sinus.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old patient presented with a right mandibular swelling of the premolar/molar area. Radiographic examination revealed periosteal duplication and 'onion-skinning'. A large periapical radiolucency was also noted on the lower right second molar. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: A young patient with a mandibular swelling, periosteal 'onion-skin' layering and a periapical infection from a molar has osteomyelitis with proliferative periostitis (Garré).

questions.stem: All of the following are features of chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis except:

options.text: Histologically, bone sclerosing and remodeling is seen
Radiographically, decreased radiodensity is seen at the involved site
Asymptomatic swelling that primarily occurs in the mandible
Histologically, it exhibits few marrow spaces coupled with a sparse or no inflammatory infiltrate

questions.explanation: Chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis INCREASES radiodensity (sclerotic bone). The other options describe it correctly.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: Periapical cyst is considered to be the most common developmental cyst. It is associated with a non-vital tooth.

options.text: The first statement is false while the second one is true
The first statement is true while the second one is false

questions.explanation: The first statement is false: the periapical cyst is the most common odontogenic cyst but it is INFLAMMATORY, not developmental (the dentigerous cyst is the most common developmental one). The second is true: it always arises on a non-vital tooth.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: The presence of mucous cells within the epithelial cyst lining is attributed to a process termed:
questions.explanation: Prosoplasia is the ability of odontogenic epithelium to show specialized differentiation, e.g. mucous cells or ciliated cells in a cyst lining.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: All of the following cysts are considered to be developmental, except:
questions.explanation: The periapical cyst is an INFLAMMATORY cyst (from the rests of Malassez stimulated by a non-vital pulp). Dermoid, thyroglossal tract and branchial cleft cysts are developmental.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: Russel bodies are mainly made of:
questions.explanation: Russel bodies are derived from degenerated plasma cells and are globules of immunoglobulin (gamma globulin).

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: The most commonly occurring cyst in the oral region is the:
questions.explanation: The radicular (periapical) cyst is the most common cyst of the jaws and oral region.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: Which of the following cysts histologically exhibits a stratified squamous epithelium of varying thickness which may contain goblet cells and cilia?
questions.explanation: The periapical cyst is lined by stratified squamous epithelium of varying thickness, which may show prosoplasia (mucous/goblet cells and cilia).

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: A thirteen-year-old patient presented to your clinic complaining of a foul taste. Examination revealed a swelling on the buccal aspect of the first permanent molar. This clinical picture is consistent with:
questions.explanation: A child (5–13 years) with a buccal swelling, foul taste and a vital first permanent molar is the buccal bifurcation cyst.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: A thirteen-year-old patient presented to your clinic complaining of a foul taste. Examination revealed a swelling on the buccal aspect of the first permanent molar. The most helpful radiograph to diagnose this case is:
questions.explanation: An occlusal radiograph best shows the buccal location of the buccal bifurcation cyst.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: A thirteen-year-old patient presented to your clinic complaining of a foul taste. Examination revealed a swelling on the buccal aspect of the first permanent molar. The treatment of this case is:

options.text: Enucleation with removal of the involved tooth
Enucleation without removal of the involved tooth
No treatment is required as the case is self limiting

questions.explanation: The buccal bifurcation cyst is treated by enucleation; extracting the involved (vital) tooth is unnecessary.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: The buccal bifurcation cyst arises as a direct consequence of the presence of:

options.text: Enamel extension into the bifurcation area

questions.explanation: The buccal bifurcation cyst is associated with an enamel extension into the bifurcation area of the mandibular first molar.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: Which of the following is considered to be the most common odontogenic cyst in the oral region?
questions.explanation: The radicular (periapical) cyst is the most common odontogenic cyst.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: Rushton bodies are seen within:
questions.explanation: Rushton bodies are curved, hyaline bodies found within the EPITHELIAL LINING of odontogenic (especially radicular) cysts. They are of vascular origin.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: Which of the following odontogenic cysts is most likely to be associated with a non-vital tooth?
questions.explanation: The periapical cyst always arises from a non-vital tooth. The others are developmental and occur with vital teeth.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: All of the following are considered to be pseudocysts except:
questions.explanation: The branchial cleft cyst is a true (lymphoepithelial) cyst with an epithelial lining. Traumatic and aneurysmal bone cysts have no epithelial lining, so they are pseudocysts.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: As a general rule of thumb, most of the diagnostic features of developmental non-odontogenic cysts exist within the connective tissue wall rather than the epithelial lining of such cysts.
questions.explanation: In developmental non-odontogenic cysts, the wall contents often make the diagnosis: nerves and vessels in the nasopalatine duct cyst, skin appendages in the dermoid, thyroid follicles in the thyroglossal cyst, lymphoid tissue in lymphoepithelial cysts.

questions.chapter: Cysts of the oral and paraoral region
questions.stem: A pseudocyst is a cavity lined by epithelium containing fluid or semi-fluid.
questions.explanation: False. A pseudocyst has NO epithelial lining; a true cyst is the one lined by epithelium.
